pages.x: In 1700 Sweden ruled an empire around the Baltic Sea, and its new king, Charles XII, was 17. Russia, Denmark and Saxony-Poland thought it was the moment to attack. They were wrong.

Charles knocked Denmark out of the war in weeks, then sailed to Narva, where some 10,000 Swedes attacked a Russian army three times their size in a snowstorm and routed it. Then he spent six years chasing Augustus of Saxony across Poland.

Peter the Great learned from defeat. He rebuilt his army on European lines, melted church bells for cannon, and in 1703 founded a city in the marshes at the mouth of the Neva, on land taken from Sweden: St Petersburg. Tens of thousands of forced labourers died building it.

In 1708 Charles marched on Moscow, but the Russians burned the land ahead of him, and the terrible winter that followed froze his army. At Poltava, in Ukraine, in June 1709, Peter destroyed it. Charles, wounded in the foot, was carried about on a stretcher.

Charles fled to the Ottoman Empire and stayed five years at Bender, urging the sultan to fight Russia. When the Ottomans finally tried to make him leave in 1713, he fought off hundreds of janissaries with a handful of men before he was captured.

Charles was shot dead in a trench in Norway in 1718. In 1721 Sweden made peace at Nystad and gave Russia Livonia, Estonia and the land around St Petersburg. Peter took a new title: Emperor of All Russia.
The war ended Sweden's days as a great power and made Russia one, with St Petersburg as its window on Europe and its capital for two centuries.
pts: Sweden against Russia and its allies, 1700 to 1721
Russia became a great European power
